Principal limitation: Equating unmistakable divine availability with coerced orientation overlooks Clifton’s distinction between recognizing a relationship and voluntarily accepting it, so the crucial disclosure-to-compulsion bridge remains unsupported, consistent with evidential warrant at 52. Live burden: Sechler needs to explain how awareness of God’s existence would involuntarily determine affection or commitment, rather than simply furnishing the prerequisite information for an unforced decision. Locked score: The overall 63 fits a relevant, understandable freedom defense whose plausible anti-coercion premise nevertheless leaves the decisive difference between knowledge and compelled relationship unresolved.

evidence.sectionTitle: Freedom, certainty, prevalence, and the goods of hiddenness

card.critique: Strongest feature: Clifton separates compelled love from awareness of a relationship; his factory-installed-certainty example answers Sechler’s freedom defense, clarifies why an undisclosed option cannot be rejected, and warrants responsiveness at 96. Principal limitation: Although the conceptual distinction is powerful, Clifton does not establish within this reply that an actual nonbeliever is nonresistant and inadequately informed, leaving the application less demonstrated and evidential warrant at 75. Live burden: Clifton needs to connect his knowledge-before-choice principle to willing nonbelievers while addressing explanations according to which divine availability can exist without unmistakable certainty. Locked score: The overall 90 properly reflects a direct and precise rebuttal that dismantles the disclosure-as-coercion equation while retaining a narrower evidentiary obligation concerning real-world cases.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But but the exercise of that free will is almost moot if we don't know that the choice exists, right? And that's the part that I'm arguing for. I'm saying, "If we don't even know that there is a God, if we don't if we don't come, you know, {quote} factory installed uh with a a certain amount of certainty that God is that God exists, he's there, he's available, he wants a relationship with us, and he loves us, and now we get to make a free choice as to whether or not to enter into that relationship, that all makes perfect sense to me. What doesn't make sense to me is, "Well, I don't want to force you to love me, so I'm not even going to let you know I'm available to be loved," right? That is the part So, there's a difference between God not forcing us to love him and God not even making his existence known in the first place. And that that second thing is is I think the prob- what the problem of non-belief is. Because you would at least have to know that God exists and is available for a relationship before you can reject that relationship. Anybody who says that I am rejecting a relationship with God, I think is misspeaking, right? It's not a relationship with God I'm rejecting. I'm rejecting the proposition that there is a God to have a relationship with in the first place. I would have to believe that God exists in order to reject a relationship with God. All I'm rejecting is a claim made by fallible human beings, right? And so I just those two things are are are very separate to me. And I think this is fundamental to the to what the problem of non-belief is, or so I see it.
